case_study_insert.main_stem: Bramblewick Free-Range Eggs (BRE) is a partnership between siblings Dan and Meg Bramble in the free-range egg farming and packing sector, employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2013, the business runs two free-range laying units and a grading and packing shed supplying cafés, farm shops and independent grocers across the region, operating a flat structure with democratic leadership. BRE plans to invest $600,000 in a second 12,000-bird free-range laying barn and upgraded packing shed, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $180,000 hire purchase for the grading machinery. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.70 a unit and a selling price of $9.50, and currently produces 105,000 units a year. BRE faces two problems: the rejection rate for cracked or blood-spot eggs has reached 6.5%, and labour turnover among weekend packers is rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Grading and Waste Report — Q3 2026: The grading line packed 27,300 boxes last quarter; the rejection rate for cracked and blood-spot eggs was 6.5%, up from 4.9% a year ago. Customer complaints about stale eggs fell from 24 to 11 per month. Average order fulfilment time is 2.4 days. A survey of 500 café and farm-shop buyers found that 61% would pay up to $0.30 more per box for free-range certified eggs, and 44% want QR-code traceability printed on boxes. The shed currently relies on quality control inspection at the end of the line, and the partners are considering quality assurance methods to prevent defects earlier. 9 of 35 staff have not completed manual egg-grading training; on-the-job coaching is available on the line, and on-site refresher courses cost $320 per employee. A quotation for a solar-powered laying barn (panels and fittings) is $48,000; grid electricity costs have risen 8.9% year-on-year.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, the fourth rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate bank facilities. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.10 to $13.91 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills for weekend packing staff. (3) Grain and soya feed costs have risen 11.6% year-on-year, and egg-price inflation is running at 7.8%, while consumer spending on free-range eggs grew 4.6% in the same period.

questions.question_text: BRE plans to fund the grading machinery with $180,000 hire purchase. Explain two advantages for BRE of hire purchase instead of funding the machinery entirely with the $420,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $180,000 cost of the grading machinery over fixed monthly instalments, so BRE keeps more of its $420,000 bank loan free for the laying barn, feed stores and wage costs during the expensive construction phase. The machinery secures its own finance, useful for a partnership whose combined borrowing is already stretched by the $600,000 expansion.

Point 2: Payments under hire purchase are matched to the useful life of the grading machinery, which is exactly how the asset generates revenue — graded boxes of 27,300 per quarter at a 6.5% rejection rate BRE badly needs to cut. BRE gets immediate use of the machine without a single large outflow, protects working capital while feed costs rise 11.6%, and gains ownership outright once the final instalment is paid, unlike an overdraft that could be called in at short notice; it also keeps the partners' personal credit untouched ahead of any future barn refinancing, and avoids pressure from the bank to shorten the $420,000 loan term once the new shed is trading.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Bramblewick Free-Range Eggs and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: BRE is launching its free-range certified box range to farm shops and cafés. Consider national television advertising, sponsorship of a regional food festival, or social media marketing aimed at local buyers. Which should BRE choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: A national TV campaign would give BRE's free-range boxes instant mass awareness and could shift national attitudes toward free-range certification. However, production and airtime costs would consume a large part of the $600,000 expansion budget, and most viewers live outside BRE's delivery region, where cafés and farm shops cannot receive boxes; for a 35-employee partnership funded by a bank loan and hire purchase, the wasted reach would be unaffordable and unmeasurable.

Sponsorship of a regional food festival: A weekend festival stall with egg cookery demonstrations reaches exactly BRE's farm-shop and café customer base face to face, lets buyers taste egg dishes, and builds the personal relationships that independent grocers value; the 61% of 500 surveyed buyers willing to pay up to $0.30 more per box can be converted on the spot with samples and QR sign-ups for traceability. The drawback is very short exposure — one weekend a year — and no scale beyond the regional catchment, so sales lift fades quickly without follow-up.

Social media marketing aimed at local buyers: Targeted posts and short videos aimed at local cafés, farm shops and conscious consumers cost little, can showcase the 6.5%-to-4.9% quality drive, the QR-code traceability that 44% of buyers want, and the $0.30 price premium story, and they reach exactly the regional catchment BRE serves, with measurable clicks to an order form. Its weakness is that reach builds slowly and depends on consistent content, and some café owners still prefer print tasting notes over social feeds.

Recommendation: BRE should choose social media marketing aimed at local buyers. It is the only option that is low-cost, targeted to the exact regional customer base, aligned with the 61% premium-willing segment and the 44% wanting QR traceability, and measurable weekly; television is rejected as too costly and geographically wasteful for a regional supplier, and festival sponsorship is rejected as a one-weekend tactic with no lasting reach, though BRE should keep a single festival stall as a complement rather than the lead promotion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of BRE with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of BRE with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and festival sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: BRE's egg rejection rate has reached 6.5%. Explain two benefits for BRE of using democratic leadership to involve packing-shed staff in reducing cracked and blood-spot eggs.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership lets the 35 employees suggest grading-line improvements — for example better light positioning at inspection tables or gentler handling of the 27,300 boxes packed last quarter — because the packers themselves see which tray positions crack the most shells. Involving them satisfies esteem needs, raises their commitment to the fix, and attacks the rejection rate directly rather than relying on end-of-line inspection alone.

Point 2: Consultation improves communication in BRE's flat structure, so problems such as the 9 of 35 staff lacking grading training surface early instead of being hidden for fear of blame. Staff who help design the solution follow it willingly, absenteeism falls, weekend packers stay longer, and BRE saves the $320 per employee refresher cost many times over as rejections drop back toward 4.9%, protecting the $9.50 price point that funds the bank-loan expansion and reinforcing the trust the partners need while staffing the second barn's weekend shifts.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BRE's rejection rate, flat structure and expansion.

questions.question_text: BRE must cut the 6.5% rejection rate. Consider quality control (end-of-line inspection) or quality assurance (prevention built into the grading process). Which should BRE choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Quality control: End-of-line inspection means trained graders checking every box after packing and downgrading cracked or blood-spot eggs before dispatch. It is simple to introduce, needs no process redesign, and matches BRE's existing routine, so stale-complaint numbers can keep falling from the current 11 per month. However, it is a detection method, not prevention: eggs are already cracked by the time they are caught, so the 4.9%-to-6.5% slide continues upstream, rejected boxes are pure cost at a $4.70 variable cost, and inspection labour is duplicated if rejections keep rising.

Quality assurance: Quality assurance builds prevention into each stage — calibrated grading machines, on-the-job coaching for the 9 untrained staff at $320 each, gentler conveyors, tray audits at the feeder and egg-quality sampling at the laying barn. It costs more up front in training, machine settings and documentation time, but it attacks root causes, so rejections fall before eggs reach the box, waste and rework disappear, and café and farm-shop customers receive consistent graded product that protects the $9.50 price and the $0.30 certification premium that 61% of buyers would pay.

Decision: BRE should adopt quality assurance as its primary approach, keeping a light end-of-line quality control check as a safety net. Prevention is the only route to reversing the 6.5% rejection rate rather than merely containing it, it fits the democratic flat structure where staff propose fixes, and its up-front cost is repaid through less waste, fewer complaints than the peak of 24 per month and stronger certification credibility for the new barn. Quality control alone is rejected because it leaves root causes untouched, locks in avoidable waste on every box packed, and would force BRE to hire more weekend graders at rising wage rates instead of solving the problem once.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of quality control and quality assurance with limited application to BRE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of both approaches in the context of BRE's rejection rate and complaints.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches in the context of BRE with a well-justified decision covering cost, waste, complaint trends and certification credibility.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how BRE's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $216,000 ÷ ($9.50 − $4.70) = $216,000 ÷ $4.80 = 45,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 45,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $9.50 − $4.70 = $4.80. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.80.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways BRE's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. BRE's partners can compare the 45,000-unit break-even output with actual production of 105,000 units to confirm the two laying units are comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 60,000 units, which supports the decision to invest $600,000 in the second barn and packing shed.
2. Contribution per unit of $4.80 lets BRE model the effect of matching the $0.30 premium that 61% of buyers will pay: raising price to $9.80 lifts contribution to $5.10, so managers can judge whether farm shops accept the increase without losing volume before printing QR traceability boxes.
3. Fixed costs of $216,000 and contribution per unit can be used to check bank-loan affordability: the $420,000 ten-year loan's repayments must be covered by the surplus of 60,000 units of safety above break-even, so the partners can test loan-term scenarios before signing with the bank.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($216,000 ÷ 105,000 units + $4.70 = $6.76 a unit) to benchmark quarterly performance, quantify the cost of the 6.5% rejection rate, and demand feed-cost efficiencies in response to the 11.6% grain and soya inflation alongside the QR traceability investment.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 45,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.80 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 60,000 units against 105,000-unit output; premium-pricing modelling from $4.80 contribution; bank-loan affordability checks on the $600,000 expansion funded by $420,000 loan and $180,000 hire purchase; and unit-cost benchmarking at $6.76 to attack the 6.5% rejection rate amid feed-cost inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BRE's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Which judgement do the figures support — has BRE's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.47 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.97 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.69 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.83 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $140,000 inventories + $90,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $265,000; 2025 current assets = $170,000 + $75,000 + $50,000 = $295,000. Short-term coverage 2024 = $265,000 ÷ $180,000 = 1.47; 2025 = $295,000 ÷ $150,000 = 1.97. Quick coverage excluding inventories 2024 = ($265,000 − $140,000) ÷ $180,000 = $125,000 ÷ $180,000 = 0.69; 2025 = ($295,000 − $170,000) ÷ $150,000 = $125,000 ÷ $150,000 = 0.83.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened. The coverage of immediate debts improved from 1.47 to 1.97, helped by current liabilities falling from $180,000 to $150,000 and cash rising to $50,000, while receivables fell from $90,000 to $75,000 as farm shops paid faster. The quick coverage rose from 0.69 to 0.83, so BRE needs stock less to meet short-term claims, although 0.83 is still below 1.0, meaning the business remains dependent on selling those 170,000 units of feed and boxed eggs to bridge any shock. Inventories rose from $140,000 to $170,000, sensible ahead of the new barn but cash-intensive, and the $420,000 bank loan plus $180,000 hire purchase will add fixed commitments that make the stronger liquidity position essential, not optional.

Conclusion: BRE's financial position has improved. Both the current ratio (1.47 to 1.97) and the acid test ratio (0.69 to 0.83) show better short-term solvency, receivables management has tightened, and the improvement is genuine rather than depending solely on inventory. The residual concern is the sub-1.0 quick coverage and rising stock, so BRE should continue tighter credit terms with cafés and farm shops and stage the barn build to protect cash before the hire-purchase instalments begin.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether BRE's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BRE of introducing a solar-powered laying barn for the new 12,000-bird unit.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A solar-powered laying barn quoting at $48,000 cuts BRE's grid electricity bill just as electricity costs have risen 8.9% year-on-year, directly protecting the $9.50 selling price and the $4.80 contribution per unit on 105,000 units a year. It also strengthens BRE's free-range and certification credentials with the 61% of surveyed buyers willing to pay up to $0.30 more per box, and the green image can be featured in the QR-code traceability material the 44% of buyers want, supporting premium farm-shop listings.

Disadvantage: The $48,000 panel cost is an extra outflow on top of the $600,000 barn budget that is already financed by a $420,000 bank loan and $180,000 hire purchase, stretching cash flow before the new unit produces a single box. Solar generation is also weather-dependent, so feed augers and lighting still need grid backup in winter months, meaning the panels will not eliminate electricity costs, and upfront maintenance or roof repairs could disrupt the 12,000-bird unit during its critical first laying cycle if panel fitting delays the barn's completion date.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BRE's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.6% rise in feed costs will affect BRE. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): BRE's $420,000 ten-year bank loan may carry a variable or repriced element, so a 0.75-point rise adds roughly $3,150 a year in interest, while the $180,000 hire purchase is fixed-rate and unaffected. Higher rates may also cool consumer spending on premium free-range boxes as households cut back, and any refinancing of the barn would now be pricier. The direct cash impact is modest but persistent, and BRE can manage part of it by fixing loan pricing early with its bank.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $13.91 per hour): BRE employs 35 staff, many in weekend grading and packing roles paid near minimum wage. A 6.2% rise adds roughly $1,700 per full-time worker per year; across a workforce of 35, with weekend casuals on top, the total payroll increase is on the order of $60,000 a year — a major pressure for a partnership whose contribution per unit is only $4.80. Democratic leadership can capture staff efficiency suggestions to offset this, but BRE must raise throughput per packer or prices to absorb the extra cost.

Input cost inflation (11.6% grain and soya feed): Feed is BRE's largest variable cost within the $4.70 per box. An 11.6% rise on the feed component adds roughly $0.35–$0.45 per box; at 105,000 boxes that is about $37,000 to $47,000 a year, cutting contribution toward $4.25–$4.35 and squeezing the margin that must service the barn loan, at exactly the moment feed volumes will rise with 12,000 more birds.

Conclusion: The 6.2% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It adds on the order of $60,000 a year to BRE's payroll across 35 staff, it cannot be avoided by reformulation or supplier switching, and it lands in the same year as the green-barn launch and grading training drive. The 11.6% feed rise is the second most serious pressure at roughly $37,000–$47,000 a year but can be partly offset by reformulating rations with nutritionists and renegotiating feed contracts; the interest-rate increase is the smallest in cash terms at a few thousand dollars and can be capped by fixing loan pricing — so BRE must respond to the wage rise first, through productivity, modest price recovery and staff retention, before defending its margin on the new barn.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to BRE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on BRE's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of BRE with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
